title: PC Maintenance
tagline: Understand a PC, maintain it safely and diagnose faults, all the way to the repair workshop.

lesson.p: It's the big board everything plugs into: processor, memory, disk… Nothing communicates without it.
The processor (CPU) is the brain: it calculates. The RAM is the working memory: it temporarily holds open programs, and empties when the PC turns off.
The disk keeps your files even when the PC is off. An HDD has spinning parts (slower, more fragile to shocks). An SSD has no moving parts: it is much faster.
The power supply unit converts the wall current into voltages suited to the PC. The fan and heatsink carry the processor's heat away.

exercises.q: Which component keeps your files when the PC is off?
exercises.why: The disk keeps data without power, unlike the RAM.

options: Temporarily holding the programs in use
exercises.why: The RAM is fast but empties at shutdown.

exercises.q: Which component converts the wall current for the PC?
exercises.hint: It is connected to the mains socket.
exercises.why: The power supply gives all components the right voltages.

exercises.q: Which component is the PC's “brain”? (3 letters)
exercises.why: The CPU (processor) carries out the calculations.

exercises.q: What is the main advantage of an SSD over an HDD?
options: It is faster and has no moving parts
exercises.why: With no moving parts, the SSD is faster and more shock-resistant.

exercises.q: Connect each component to the motherboard.
exercises.hint: Everything connects to the motherboard, in the centre.
exercises.why: The motherboard is the centre: everything communicates through it.

lesson.p: Before opening a PC, switch it off and unplug the mains cable. Then hold the power button for a few seconds to drain the remaining electricity.
Your body can build up a charge and fry a component. Touch a metal part of the case before touching the motherboard, and never put components on synthetic fabric.

Dust blocks the air and makes the PC hot. Blow it away with compressed air or a small blower, holding the fan with a finger so it doesn't spin too fast. Don't use an ordinary vacuum cleaner, it creates static electricity.
Install updates, keep an antivirus, and back up your important files to a USB stick or another disk: a disk can fail without warning.

exercises.q: Before opening a PC, what do you do first?
options: I switch it off and unplug the mains cable
exercises.why: A plugged-in PC can be dangerous and damage components.

exercises.q: Why touch a metal part of the case before touching the motherboard?
options: To discharge the static electricity from your body
exercises.why: A static discharge can destroy a component without you seeing it.

exercises.q: Put these in order to dust a PC safely.
lines: Switch off the PC and unplug the mains cable
Blow the dust away while holding the fan
Close the case and plug back in
exercises.hint: You must cut the power first.
exercises.why: Cut the power, open, clean, then reassemble.

exercises.q: Why hold the fan with a finger when blowing on it?
options: So it doesn't spin too fast and get damaged
exercises.hint: A fan spinning too fast can get damaged.
exercises.why: Compressed air would make it spin far too fast.

exercises.q: Which tool do you avoid for cleaning inside a PC?
exercises.why: An ordinary vacuum cleaner can generate static electricity.

options: A disk can fail without warning
exercises.why: A backup stops you losing everything if the disk fails.

lesson.p: Look and listen: do the lights come on? Is the fan spinning? Are there beeps? What you observe points to the cause.

Nothing lights up: power supply or mains cable. Black screen with beeps: often badly seated RAM. The PC switches off by itself after a while: overheating, often because of dust. The PC is very slow: disk almost full or too many apps.
Start with the causes that are easy to check: socket, cables, connections. Never replace an expensive part without testing the simple causes first.
In the exercises, tap the tests to carry them out, read the observations, then pick the cause. Do several tests before answering.

exercises.q: A PC doesn't switch on at all. Investigate.

cmds.c: Test the socket with a charger
cmds.out: A phone charger works on this socket.

cmds.c: Inspect the inside and the connections
cmds.out: The power cable is half out at the back of the PC.

options: The power cable is badly plugged in
exercises.hint: Test the socket and cables first.
exercises.why: The socket works and the cable isn't pushed in: simply plugging it back in fixes the fault.

cmds.out: Black screen. The PC gives 3 short repeated beeps.

cmds.c: Inspect the inside and the connections
cmds.out: A RAM stick isn't fully pushed into its slot.

options: A RAM stick is badly seated
exercises.hint: Beeps at start-up point to the memory.
exercises.why: Black screen + beeps + badly seated stick: push it back in.

exercises.q: The PC switches itself off after ten minutes. Investigate.

cmds.out: The PC starts but switches itself off after a few minutes.
Very noisy fan, burning hot air coming out of the case.

cmds.c: Inspect the inside and the connections
cmds.out: The fan and heatsink are covered in dust.

options: The screen is badly plugged in
exercises.hint: Burning air and noise: what's going on?
exercises.why: Dust blocks the air: the PC overheats and protects itself by switching off.

exercises.q: The PC takes three minutes to start. Investigate.

cmds.out: The PC starts but very slowly.

cmds.c: Inspect the inside and the connections
cmds.out: The inside is clean, everything is in place.

options: The mains cable is badly plugged in
exercises.why: An almost full disk slows everything down: free up some space.

exercises.q: A PC won't start. What do you check first?
options: The socket and the power cables
exercises.why: We start with the simple, easy-to-check causes.

exercises.q: Black screen and several beeps at start-up: which component do you suspect first?
exercises.hint: The beeps are a code from the motherboard.
exercises.why: Start-up beeps often signal a memory problem.

lesson.p: Customers have dropped off 8 machines at the workshop. 4 of them are broken. It's up to you to test each one, understand the fault and choose the right repair.
For each broken machine: switch it on, listen to the fan, inspect the inside and the connections, and check the disk. Read the observations, then choose the matching repair.
Changing the motherboard or reinstalling Windows almost never fixes a simple fault: it wastes time (and points). Look for the real cause first.

exercises.q: 4 workshop machines are broken (in red). Tap a machine, run the tests, then repair it.
exercises.hint: Compare what the switch-on, the fan, the inspection and the disk show.
exercises.why: Four faults, four different causes: power cable, RAM, dust and a full disk.

plug: No light, no sound: the machine is dead.
The power cable is half out of the back of the machine.
ram: A RAM stick isn't fully pushed into its slot.
dust: The machine starts but switches itself off after a few minutes.
Very noisy fan, burning hot air coming out of the machine.
The fan and heatsink are covered in dust.
disk: The machine starts but very slowly (3 minutes).
The inside is clean, everything is in place.
Disk C: 99% used (1 GB left). The machine is saturated.

repairs.label: Plug the power cable back in
Push the RAM stick back in
